flashcards.front: What does a physical access log record?
flashcards.back_definition: Each badge use at a controlled door: time, badge ID, door, and whether access was granted or denied.
flashcards.back_confusion: A valid swipe proves a credential was used, not that its owner used it.

flashcards.front: Name four suspicious patterns in an access log.
flashcards.back_definition: Entries outside the person's schedule, a burst of denials on one badge, one badge at two distant doors too quickly, and one swipe where a sensor counts two people.
flashcards.back_example: Badge 2201 is denied 6 times in 40 seconds at the lab door.
flashcards.back_confusion: Logs alone miss tailgating: the person following never swipes. Door counters or cameras catch it.
flashcards.back_hook: Wrong time, too many tries, impossible travel, extra bodies.

flashcards.back_definition: A rule that refuses entry to a badge that has not been used to exit since it last entered, which exposes badges being passed back to someone else.
flashcards.back_example: An employee enters, hands the badge back out through a window, and the second entry is refused.
flashcards.back_confusion: Anti-passback works only if exits are badged as well as entries.
flashcards.back_hook: In, then out, then in again.

flashcards.back_definition: The same credential used at two places too far apart for one person to travel between in the time recorded, which suggests a cloned or shared badge.
flashcards.back_example: Badge 9001 enters Building A at 09:00:05 and Building C, a ten-minute walk away, at 09:01:10.
flashcards.back_confusion: The same idea is used for online logins from two countries minutes apart.

flashcards.front: How do logs become an active detective control?
flashcards.back_definition: A SIEM checks events as they arrive against rules and alerts within seconds, instead of logs only being read after an incident.
flashcards.back_example: An after-hours entry to the server room pages the on-call guard immediately.
flashcards.back_confusion: Stored but unread logs only help the investigation afterwards.

flashcards.front: Name the main parts of an intrusion alarm system.
flashcards.back_definition: Sensors (door and window contacts, glass-break, motion), a control panel that knows the arm state, sirens or silent signals, and a monitoring centre that verifies and dispatches.
flashcards.back_example: A door contact trips while the system is armed; the central station calls the keyholder, then police.
flashcards.back_confusion: An alarm detects and responds; it does not physically stop entry.

flashcards.front: What are entry and exit delays for?
flashcards.back_definition: Grace periods that let a legitimate person leave after arming, or reach the keypad and disarm after coming in, without causing a false alarm.
flashcards.back_example: 30 seconds after the front door opens to type the code.
flashcards.back_confusion: Entry delay applies only on the normal entry route; a window opening while armed alarms at once.
flashcards.back_hook: Time to get the keys out.

flashcards.back_definition: Treating an event as confirmed only when two independent sensors or zones trip within a short time, which cuts false dispatches.
flashcards.back_example: A hallway motion sensor and a server-room door contact both trip within 60 seconds.
flashcards.back_confusion: It reduces false alarms but must not slow down panic or duress alarms.

flashcards.front: Why does a panic or duress button skip normal checks?
flashcards.back_definition: A person pressing it is already a high-confidence signal of danger, so it goes straight to dispatch whatever the arm state.
flashcards.back_example: A cashier presses a hidden button during a robbery.
flashcards.back_confusion: Panic buttons are mostly about personal safety, not burglary.
flashcards.back_hook: A human press is its own verification.

flashcards.front: How does a PIR motion sensor work?
flashcards.back_definition: A passive infrared sensor detects a change in heat across parts of its field of view. It emits nothing itself.
flashcards.back_example: A warm body crossing the room changes the infrared pattern and trips the sensor.
flashcards.back_confusion: Microwave sensors are active: they send a signal and detect the Doppler shift from moving objects.
flashcards.back_hook: PIR feels heat move; microwave bounces signals.

flashcards.front: What is a dual-technology motion sensor?
flashcards.back_definition: A sensor that combines two methods, usually PIR and microwave, and alerts only when both trigger together, which cuts false positives.
flashcards.back_example: A heating vent fools the PIR, but the microwave sees no movement, so no alarm.
flashcards.back_confusion: Requiring both can miss a slow, careful intruder; placement and tuning still matter.

flashcards.front: Why is maximum sensor sensitivity not maximum security?
flashcards.back_definition: Very high sensitivity catches pets, insects, air currents and sunlight, so staff learn to ignore alarms or switch sensors off.
flashcards.back_example: After weeks of false alerts from a fan, guards stop responding to that zone.
flashcards.back_confusion: Tuning trades missed detections against false alarms; neither extreme is safe.
flashcards.back_hook: Cry wolf often enough and nobody comes.

flashcards.front: Why place detection in layers and zones?
flashcards.back_definition: Overlapping sensors in perimeter and interior zones show where an intruder is and still catch them if one layer is bypassed.
flashcards.back_example: Fence sensor, then door contact, then server-room motion: three chances to detect.
flashcards.back_confusion: A single sensor has blind spots; overlap covers them.
flashcards.back_hook: Catch them at the fence, the door or the room.

flashcards.front: Detect, assess, respond: why do all three matter?
flashcards.back_definition: Detection without assessment floods guards with noise, and assessment without a timely response just watches the attack happen.
flashcards.back_example: A loading-dock camera blind spot and a slow response let thieves leave before anyone arrives.
flashcards.back_confusion: Detection is only worth as much as the response that follows.
flashcards.back_hook: See it, judge it, act on it.
